doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Coltrane's sales and appeal
summary: He disputes Coltrane's record sales and says Wild Bill Moore thought Ascension sounded like a wounded rhinoceros.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Well, he did sell a lot of records. You don’t agree?
Ah...I don’t know about a lot of records. I mean, you hear them on the jazz station. He didn’t sell no records.
we don’t have enough time to debate it, but A Love Supreme sold a lot of records.
Yeah. That’s just a lot of BS. Herb Alpert had ten straight one-million-dollar record-sellers. Did he do that?
If you’re talking about selling records. Selling records is selling records.
In your opinion, why do you think Coltrane struck such a chord with a lot of people in the jazz public, younger people particularly, during the ‘60s?

Well, he’s a junkie. Any time you see a junkie, and people like that. They like that. He used to play one chorus for an hour. That’s not no... And he played a lot of harmonics and technical things. Got nothing to do with jazz. Jazz, you can play one or two notes on a tune. You don’t think so, you listen to Gene Ammons. I used to see Gene and Sonny. Sonny used to eat Gene up playing stuff. Sonny was a technician. Gene played two or three notes. People didn’t even want to hear Sonny any more.
You’re kind of a cross between Gene Ammons and Sonny Stitt.

Well, that’s what I said. I’m one of the in-between musicians. I try both sides. See, Trane... I listened to Trane... I took one of the old saxophone players, Wild Bill Moore. Now, he used to rock-and-roll, walking the bar, all that kind of saxophone playing. I let him hear “Ascension.” So he listened to it. I said, “What you think?” He said, “He sounds like a wounded rhinoceros that somebody shot and left out in the woods and died.”
